title: "Visualising missingness and imputation"
output: rmarkdown::html_vignette
vignette: >
  %\VignetteIndexEntry{Visualising missingness and imputation}
  %\VignetteEngine{knitr::rmarkdown}
  %\VignetteEncoding{UTF-8}
---

```{r setup, message=FALSE}
library(pigauto)
data(avonet300, tree300)
set.seed(42)
tree <- ape::keep.tip(tree300, sample(tree300$tip.label, 80))
traits <- avonet300[match(tree$tip.label, avonet300$Species_Key),
                    c("Mass", "Wing.Length", "Trophic.Level",
                      "Primary.Lifestyle"), drop = FALSE]
rownames(traits) <- tree$tip.label
traits$Mass[1:8] <- NA
traits$Wing.Length[6:13] <- NA
traits$Trophic.Level[4:11] <- NA
traits$Primary.Lifestyle[10:17] <- NA
x <- preprocess_traits(traits, tree)
```

Imagine assembling a comparative dataset of bird body mass, wing length,
trophic level and lifestyle. The first two are continuous measurements; the
last two are categorical traits. Here we use 80 birds from the bundled AVONET
data and deliberately remove some entries to make the example reproducible.
The gaps are assigned by position in the tree's tip order, so they can cluster
among relatives. They illustrate the plots; they do not reproduce a known
real-world missingness process. Start with the missingness plots to decide
whether the available measurements are distributed across the tree or
concentrated in particular groups.

Before fitting, compare missing fractions and inspect the observation-by-trait matrix. Labels include trait types; each expanded categorical trait is represented once.

```{r, fig.height=6, fig.width=8, out.width="100%"}
plot_missingness(x, "summary")
plot_missingness(x, "matrix")
```

The tree-ordered matrix places related tips close together, helping reveal clades with more missing data. The co-missingness map reports the fraction of all observations missing each pair of traits, including the marginal fraction on its diagonal. Such patterns guide investigation; neither plot establishes the missingness mechanism or proves data are missing completely at random.

```{r, fig.height=6, fig.width=8, out.width="100%"}
plot_missingness(x, "phylo", tree)
plot_missingness(x, "co_missing")
```

## Inspecting individual predictions

Fit the mixed traits together, then inspect the predicted mass and its
conformal bounds for a few birds whose mass we removed. The bounds are on the
original mass scale, so they can be read alongside the prediction. They give
an exploratory sense of the range of plausible values for an individual
missing measurement, which can help decide which values need closer scrutiny.
The same dataset also contains categorical traits, but these numeric
conformal bounds are not categorical confidence intervals. Here the true
mass is known because we removed it ourselves; in a real application it would
need to be measured independently to check an individual prediction.

```{r fit-plots, message=FALSE, fig.width=8, fig.height=5}
result <- impute(traits, tree, gnn = FALSE, verbose = FALSE, seed = 7)
missing_mass <- which(is.na(traits$Mass))
mass_predictions <- data.frame(
  species = rownames(traits)[missing_mass],
  predicted_mass_g = result$prediction$imputed[missing_mass, "Mass"],
  lower_g = result$prediction$conformal_lower[missing_mass, "Mass"],
  upper_g = result$prediction$conformal_upper[missing_mass, "Mass"],
  hidden_mass_g = avonet300$Mass[match(rownames(traits)[missing_mass],
                                       avonet300$Species_Key)],
  row.names = NULL
)
mass_predictions
```

Plot just the missing masses, using a log scale because bird masses span a
wide range. The dot is the point prediction, the line its exploratory
conformal interval, and the cross the measurement we deliberately hid. In an
actual dataset the cross would be unavailable for a genuinely missing value.
An especially broad interval, or a hidden value outside its interval, prompts
closer investigation rather than unquestioning reliance on the imputation.

```{r mass-intervals, fig.width=8, fig.height=5}
ggplot2::ggplot(mass_predictions,
  ggplot2::aes(x = predicted_mass_g, y = species,
               xmin = lower_g, xmax = upper_g)) +
  ggplot2::geom_pointrange(orientation = "y") +
  ggplot2::geom_point(ggplot2::aes(x = hidden_mass_g),
                      shape = 4, colour = "#B33A3A", size = 2.5) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_log10() +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "Predicted body mass (g; log scale)", y = NULL,
                title = "Missing body masses: predictions and exploratory intervals") +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal()
```

In this particular example, none of the eight hidden masses falls inside its
interval. The greater rhea's hidden mass is 23,000 g, while its predicted mass
is about 1,529 g. The eight were chosen by tree position and include very large
and very small birds: the rhea is larger than every remaining observed bird,
and one hummingbird is smaller than all of them. Their prediction errors are
large relative to the calibration errors. These eight selected gaps are not
an independent random sample, so their 0/8 coverage is not an estimate of
general performance. The red crosses are possible here only because we started
with recorded values and hid them ourselves.

The fit also warns that only **six mass observations** were available to
calibrate the interval score. That is too few to support the usual finite-sample
95% split-conformal guarantee with a finite empirical bound, even before
considering whether the calibration and missing species are exchangeable.
We show the warning deliberately: inspect it when interpreting your own fit.

These are prediction intervals for missing trait values, not confidence
intervals for a regression coefficient. Their nominal 95% coverage is not
certified for this dataset. Standard conformal coverage depends on calibration
and future cases being exchangeable; related species, clade-structured
missingness and differences between observed and missing species can make
that assumption questionable. A small calibration set also makes the bounds
unstable, and wide bounds can cover values while offering little practical
precision. Examine held-out coverage **and** interval width, using the number
of test values and species- or clade-level holdouts relevant to your question.
The single fit above does not establish 95% coverage.

For a categorical trait, inspect the predicted class separately. Here are the
birds with an artificially missing trophic level. These labels are point
predictions; a numeric mass interval does not quantify their class uncertainty.

```{r categorical-predictions}
missing_diet <- which(is.na(traits$Trophic.Level))
data.frame(
  species = rownames(traits)[missing_diet],
  predicted_trophic_level = result$prediction$imputed[missing_diet, "Trophic.Level"],
  hidden_trophic_level = avonet300$Trophic.Level[
    match(rownames(traits)[missing_diet], avonet300$Species_Key)],
  row.names = NULL
)
```

The hidden labels let us see individual mistakes in this demonstration. In
practice, use a separate held-out evaluation to assess accuracy and compare it
with a simple baseline; do not read these eight examples as a performance study.

Conformal scores are quantiles of held-out errors on an encoded trait scale;
they help construct bounds but do not measure prediction accuracy or establish
coverage on their own. Conformal-based multiple-imputation draws are for
prediction diagnostics, not Rubin pooling. For downstream estimates and
confidence intervals, use a supported analysis-aware or posterior multiple-
imputation route, and check its documented scope and validation limitations.
Eligibility for pooling does not itself establish reliable inference for your
analysis; see the [validation results](validation-results.html).

## Checking prediction accuracy

Use held-out observed values to assess point predictions. For example:

```{r evaluation, message=FALSE}
evaluate(result$fit)
```

## Reading the prediction metrics

The test values are observations that pigauto deliberately hid before fitting.
Their true values remain available for checking predictions. They are different
from the genuinely missing values, whose prediction errors we cannot measure
without collecting new observations. Use `evaluate(result$fit)` for this check.
If you need a prediction object for lower-level scoring, request
`predict(result$fit, evaluation = TRUE)`; production predictions may use the
observed values you would otherwise be treating as hidden.

| Metric | Meaning | How to read it |
|---|---|---|
| RMSE on the standardized latent scale (zRMSE) | Square root of the average squared difference between predictions and hidden values, after the trait's transformation and standardization. | Smaller is better; zero means exact agreement on these cells. A value of 0.5 is half a preprocessing standard deviation on this scale, not half an original measurement unit. Squaring gives larger errors more weight. |
| Accuracy for binary or categorical traits | Fraction of hidden class labels predicted correctly. | Larger is better; 0.8 means 80% correct. Compare with the majority-class prediction: 80% accuracy is uninformative if predicting the commonest class already achieves 90%. |
| Correlation | How predictions and hidden values vary together. | High correlation does not rule out a systematic shift or an incorrect prediction scale. Inspect error measures too. |
| Conformal score | A high quantile of absolute validation errors, used to set prediction-bound width for supported traits. | It is measured on the encoded trait scale. A larger value gives wider bounds; it does not by itself demonstrate that those bounds cover missing values at the nominal rate. |
| Held-out coverage | Fraction of hidden test values inside the reported bounds. | Read it with the number of test values and interval width. A small test set gives an imprecise coverage estimate; broad bounds can cover many values without being useful. |

For continuous, count, ordinal and proportion traits, `evaluate()` reports
RMSE on the encoded scale. Depending on the trait, that scale uses log,
log1p, integer ranks or logit before standardization. The HTML report labels
this "RMSE (latent scale)". The standardization makes units explicit but
provides no universal good/bad threshold: compare predictions on the same
hidden cells with a suitable simple reference and consider the biological
cost of an error. Other metrics, such as zero-inflated-count RMSE and
compositional errors, have their own scales; see `?evaluate_imputation`.

A point prediction and an individual completed-data draw answer different
questions. Score the point prediction to assess its error. To assess a
predictive distribution, consider coverage together with width or a suitable
distributional score. Scoring each stochastic completion adds its draw
variation to prediction error; that alone does not establish whether the
uncertainty is appropriate. `mi$pooled_point` is the selected route's point
completion, not generally an average of the returned `m` datasets.
